## Incident Report — Koi Stealer Infection, DESKTOP-RNVO9AT

**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-09-04-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (5,091 frames, ~59.6 min capture), `2024-09-04-traffic-analysis-exercise-alerts.txt`, `2024-09-04-traffic-analysis-exercise-alerts.jpg`

### Victim host

| Attribute | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 172.17.0.99 | consistent across all evidence |
| MAC | 18:3d:a2:b6:8d:c4 | ARP (172.17.0.99 ↔ 18:3d:a2:b6:8d:c4), matches DHCP client MAC |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-RNVO9AT | DHCP option 12, NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` records, DNS self-registration query `DESKTOP-RNVO9AT.bepositive.com` |
| Logged-in user | **afletcher** (Andrew Fletcher) | Kerberos `CNameString` (both TGT request/reply legs, .99 ↔ .17); LDAP `givenName=Andrew`, `sn=Fletcher` in a bind against the DC |
| AD domain / DC | bepositive.com, DC WIN-CTL9XBQ9Y19.bepositive.com | DNS SRV lookups (`_ldap._tcp...dc._msdcs.bepositive.com`), NBNS `WIN-CTL9XBQ9Y19<20>` at 172.17.0.17 (MAC 00:23:ae:50:ba:fd) |

The host is a domain-joined Windows workstation (SMBv1/NetBIOS browser-election traffic, `NetServerEnum2`, Kerberos auth) on the 172.17.0.0/24 LAN, with 172.17.0.17 as its DC and internal DNS server.

### Malware family

**Koi Stealer (Win32/Koi Stealer).** Attribution is **signature-confirmed**: the Suricata/ET alert export contains `ETPRO TROJAN Win32/Koi Stealer CnC Checkin (POST) M2` (48 hits) fired directly against the C2 traffic from 172.17.0.99 to 79.124.78.197, corroborated by `ET INFO GENERIC SUSPICIOUS POST to Dotted Quad with Fake Browser 1` (50 hits) on the same stream.

Behavioral confirmation from the pcap itself:
- Repeated `POST /foots.php HTTP/1.1` to bare-IP host `79.124.78.197`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, body starting with a stable bot ID `30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654` (e.g. `101|30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654|5LHtVruc|...`).
- Static fake User-Agent on every request: `Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 10.0; WOW64; Trident/7.0; ...)` — an outdated IE7 string spoofed on a Windows 10 host.
- Regular beaconing cadence: bursts of 3 requests ~0.7s apart, then a steady interval of ~60–70s, continuing from 17:35 UTC through the end of the capture (22:31 UTC), i.e. persistent post-infection C2.

A second channel to the same IP, `/index.php?id=&subid=qIOuKk7U` (GET then POST with an encrypted-looking body), is **behavioral only, not signature-named** — it looks like a loader/PPI gate check-in (response contains token `HckDcK0czXjaq48jVHNn` and echoes the `subid`), likely shared infrastructure with the stealer C2 but not independently confirmed by any signature.

### Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint (signature-confirmed):**
- `79.124.78.197:80` — HTTP, `POST /foots.php` (Koi Stealer CnC checkin channel)
- `79.124.78.197:80` — HTTP, `GET/POST /index.php` (`?id=&subid=qIOuKk7U`) — secondary loader/gate channel, behavioral attribution only

No DNS lookup for 79.124.78.197 appears anywhere in the capture — the malware connects to this IP hardcoded, so there is no associated C2 domain to report.

**Bot/session identifier:** `30168213-3be0-a751-81a0-cf3b228c8654` (sent in every `/foots.php` POST body)

**Likely payload-delivery precursor (behavioral, unconfirmed — timing correlation only):**
- `46.254.34.201:443` — TLS, SNI `www.bellantonicioccolato.it`. This session starts at capture time 153.3s and completes ~700 KB of server→client transfer by 154.4s, 1.8 seconds before the first `/foots.php` C2 beacon at 155.4s. No DNS query for this domain appears in the capture (also hardcoded), and the transfer is TLS-encrypted, so no file name or hash could be recovered. Flagged as a probable second-stage payload fetch based on size and timing, not confirmed.

**Files / hashes:** None recoverable. All malicious traffic observed is either raw binary HTTP POST bodies (no discrete named object, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`) or TLS-encrypted — no SHA256 could be computed from this capture.

### Ruled out / benign context (not IOCs)

- `www.msftconnecttest.com` (23.220.251.149/.158), `dns.msftncsi.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, `x1.c.lencr.org`, `acroipm2.adobe.com` (`/assets/Owner/arm/ProcessMAU.txt`, 4-byte Adobe updater response), and the large volume of `*.msn.com`, `bing.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `officeapps.live.com` traffic — standard Windows/Office/Adobe telemetry and connectivity checks.
- `ET INFO Terse Request for .txt - Likely Hostile` and `ET INFO Microsoft Connection Test` alerts against 23.220.251.149 — false-positive matches on the legitimate Windows NCSI probe (`GET /connecttest.txt`, 200 OK, 22-byte plaintext response).
- `GPL NETBIOS SMB Session Setup NTMLSSP unicode asn1 overflow attempt`, `GPL NETBIOS SMB IPC$ unicode share access`, `GPL NETBIOS SMB_COM_TRANSACTION Max Data Count of 0 DOS Attempt`, `GPL RPC kerberos principal name overflow TCP` (all 172.17.0.99 → 172.17.0.17) — inspected the underlying SMB commands directly: standard SMB1 Negotiate/Session-Setup/Tree-Connect(`IPC$`)/`NetServerEnum2`/Logoff sequence, i.e. routine NetBIOS browser-election and AD authentication traffic. These are generic legacy signatures known to false-positive on normal domain-joined Windows chatter; no evidence of exploitation was found in the packet content.
